entries.title: I want a battle, I WANT A WAR
entries.summary: The owner played the build and asked for scale. The session opened with a backlog, a measured foundation, a PRD built on five pillars, and 74 issue specs decomposed across seven epics — reviewable in git before a single one became a GitHub issue.

commits.subject: docs: theatre-scale backlog — 22 items across four phases
docs: output rules, the theatre-scale PRD, and an issue pipeline
docs: 74 issue specs for theatre scale, projected into GitHub
docs(issues): make the dependency graph say what it means

body.text: Latticefall today is a competent tower defence with one genuinely good idea: power is the real currency. The largest board is 18x15 tiles, peak screen presence is 32 units, one lane, one entrance, one exit, and a fixed list of eight to twelve places you are allowed to build. The owner played it and said what they wanted next, in their own words:
I want a battle, I WANT A WAR.

Theatre Scale is the programme that turns a screen into a battlefield. It rests on five pillars: ground you cannot cover, build where you want (no fixed slots), terrain that means something (elevation and bridges), weapons you can see from across the valley (spectacle as different **shapes** of power draw, never just bigger numbers), and power as a front line — supply you build, route, and defend.

One rule outranks all five. The rules of the game exist twice — `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` for the engine, `sim/engine.py` as the reference — and a parity harness diffs them on every commit: 864 runs when this session opened, 1,152 by the time it closed. That is what makes any balance claim in this project falsifiable, and every entry after this one either keeps both implementations in step or says plainly that it does not.
74 issues, seven epics, no cycles

rows: camera and reading a big board
multi-lane, mass and the war economy
balance that can see the game

body.text: The specs live in `docs/issues/*.md` and are the source of truth; GitHub is a projection built by `tools/issues.py`, so a lost repository or a rate limit costs nothing — re-run it and the issues come back identical. Twenty-two of the seventy-four could start with nothing blocking them.

The dependency graph was checked rather than trusted. `tools/issues.py` derives 'blocks' from 'depends', and the two had drifted: of thirteen hand-written 'blocks' claims, ten were either transitive or simply wrong — one asserted it blocked work the plan deliberately wanted running in parallel. Three were real, and became depends edges instead, which is the side that actually counts.

Four traps surfaced before a single issue was implemented, all found by reading the code the specs would touch rather than by writing the specs first and finding out later. The parity outcome signature encodes tower positions as `%s@%d,%d` in both engines, and free placement makes those floats — the grader's candidate positions would need pinning to a binary fraction to round-trip identically between languages. The parity test harness turned out to carry its own private copy of two build-placement functions, making the free-placement work a three-file change rather than two. Sprite yaw slots are named `y%03d` and the heading function returns a plain integer, and sixteen directions are 22.5 degrees apart — half of them not whole numbers — so that naming has to become bucket indices before a single new asset can render. And one rules file justifies a piece of bookkeeping 'because records are only ever compared by slot' — free placement removes the slot, so that invariant needs a new basis at the same moment it needs everything else.

Nothing above was built yet. It was the day the plan got measured instead of argued — which is also the subject of the entry that follows, and which happened, in fact, a little earlier the same evening.

entries.title: Seven defects, measured before a line of the plan was written
entries.summary: Profiling the real code against synthetic boards and unit counts, rather than guessing what would break on the way to a war-scale board. The whole game today costs 1.5 ms of a 16.7 ms frame — so the question was never whether there is headroom, only which thing runs out first.

commits.subject: docs: measured scale limits — 7 defects found profiling the theatre-scale plan

body.text: Before a single Theatre Scale issue was implemented, the real code was profiled against synthetic boards and unit counts, to find out what actually breaks on the way to a war-scale board rather than guessing. The whole game today costs 1.5 ms of a 16.7 ms frame — so the question was never whether there is headroom, only which thing runs out first.
Four defects already shipping

items: An idle emplacement with nothing in range re-scans every unit on the board, every tick, forever — the empty-target path never resets its own cooldown. Measured **2.19x** the cost of the same board with targets in range at 8 towers / 32 units, rising to **2.87x** at 100 / 800.

`_covered_by()` tests every placed emplacement's effect type inside its own loop, so it costs O(towers) per unit even when nothing on the board has that effect at all — **24,000** wasted iterations per tick at 60 towers and 400 units.
The hit-flash lookup scans the entire live hit list for every drawn unit, roughly U^1.9 — **29%** of all draw cost at 900 units.
`drawables()` is rebuilt and re-sorted **four times a frame** — once each for the shadow pass, the sprite pass, the glow layer and the additive FX layer.

body.text: Three that block the plan, not the game

items: `render.py`'s `calibrate()` cannot converge at 384px or 1024px cells — it corrects orthographic scale from the width ratio only, so a one-pixel height shortfall never resolves. 256 and 512 only work by luck.
The board-saturation guard reads a tower's base `draw_mw` and never its `upgrade.draw_mw`, so an upgraded tower's real draw is invisible to the check that exists to protect the power decision.

Sprite legibility at zoom-out is a design question, not a camera feature. Fitting a 64x64 board needs **0.234x** zoom at 100% interface scale and **0.117x** at 200% — rendering a sprite at 30 to 60 px, likely below the point where one enemy is distinguishable from another. That needs a human answer before a camera can be built around it.

body.text: Also recorded, and revisited within a day: both rule engines compute lane-segment length as `abs(dx)+abs(dy)`, with no square root anywhere, because Python's and Godot's floating point are not guaranteed bit-identical — decision 030's reasoning, and the reason the parity gate has stayed green. Diagonal lanes would reopen that question, so the axis-aligned rule was written down rather than quietly assumed safe forever. It would turn out to be half wrong the very next day — see decision 061, in the entry on the gate.
None of these seven were fixed here. They were found so that everything built afterward would be built on what the code actually does, not on what it was assumed to do.

entries.title: The board you cannot fit on a screen
entries.summary: anchor-24's board draws 2,112 px wide against a 940 px strip between the two instrument panels — and 4 px at 200% interface scale. Fixing that needed a camera, and the camera needed an answer nobody could measure their way out of: how much detail is allowed to disappear when the whole board finally fits.

commits.subject: refactor(view): the backdrop stops being a child of the board
feat(view): a board camera — pan, zoom, edge-scroll, cursor-follow
docs: measure the legibility floor instead of arguing about it
docs: record decision 056 — zoom-out buys the whole board, not detail

body.text: anchor-24's board draws 2,112 px wide against a 940 px strip between the two instrument panels at 100% interface scale — and **4 px** at 200%. The panels do not crowd the board at that scale; they erase it. Fixing that needed a camera, and the camera needed an answer to a question nobody could measure their way out of: how much detail is allowed to disappear when the whole board finally fits on screen?
Three transforms, kept separate

The board could not simply be scaled. The sky backdrop sized itself to the raw viewport and was a child of the board's own node, so zooming the board would have stretched the sky and torn the full-bleed gradient off the screen edges. The backdrop moved to be a sibling instead, which freed the board's own scale for zoom and a separate origin term for pan, while position stayed reserved for screen shake — three transform terms, three separate jobs, verified pixel-identical before and after across four interface-scale and anchor combinations, then confirmed live by nudging the board's scale at runtime and watching the sky stay full-bleed and unmoved.

`ZOOM_MIN` is derived, not authored: it fits whatever board is loaded into the visible strip, recomputed on load, so it is already correct for a board nobody has built yet. Pan is a middle-drag rather than a left-drag, because left click already arms builds and selects emplacements. Verified as frames and numbers rather than argued: mouse picking resolved to the exact predicted tile at zoom 0.5, wheel-zoom held the point under the cursor to within 0.3 px, and the HUD's own accessibility report differed in **0 of 36 items** between zoom 1.0 and the new zoom floor — the thing most likely to have broken quietly, since the type ladder and palette were solved for contrast at one known size.
The legibility question, measured rather than argued

body.caption: Every drawn tower and enemy at 30, 45, 60 and 90 px, sampled against the real board tile colour rather than an authored swatch. No pair of the 22 drawn ids collapses by silhouette at any of these sizes — the closest pair is flak-array against pulse-turret, at a Jaccard overlap of 0.158. What the matrix cannot see, and this sheet shows plainly, is that the real loss at 30 to 45 px is interior colour and detail, not outline.

The same board downsampled to the zoom floor at both interface scales — a proxy for a camera that did not exist yet at the moment this was measured. At 0.117x, the floor at 200% interface scale, a 256 px atlas cell lands at 30 to 60 px on screen.

body.text: Decision 056: zoom-out buys the whole board, not detail

Three options were costed: raise the tile size project-wide; float the zoom minimum and let a minimap carry the wide read; or re-author the sprite library silhouette-first so it survives 30 px. The owner's answer settled it: they would be excited if an item stayed legible zoomed all the way out, but would not be upset if a lot of detail were lost at that distance. So the zoom floor fits the board, not the sprite, and a minimap — a separate entry later in this journal — carries the wide read instead.

That killed both of the expensive options outright. Raising the tile size touches every screen-space calculation in the project, the measured sprite pivot, the atlas packer's fixed cell, the render pipeline's orthographic-scale formula, and the accessibility baselines sampled from the composited frame — and it was blocked behind the `calibrate()` convergence defect from the previous entry besides. Re-authoring the library silhouette-first would have spent the art budget at the zoom level where the player is reading lane pressure, not identifying unit types. It also settled a second open question for free: board size is no longer constrained by what the art can show at full zoom-out, so it can be chosen on gameplay and performance grounds alone.

entries.title: The gate: eleven minutes, five seconds, and a check for every failure that already happened
entries.summary: tools/check.py was 18 checks and roughly eleven minutes, every time — run at the end of a task rather than during it, exactly when it is least useful. By the time this session closed it was 27 checks with a five-second first tier, running in CI, and enforcing two things that had already gone wrong once.

commits.subject: feat(gate): enumerate from git, parse every script, and emit JSON
feat(gate): tier the gate, and wire the terrain parity check into it
ci: a gate that runs somewhere other than this machine
perf(gate): parity skips when nothing that can change it changed, and shards when it must
feat(gate): three checks for three failures that already happened
feat(gate): check the hooks, both directions of asset coverage, and the facing harness

body.text: The gate — `tools/check.py` — was 18 checks and roughly eleven minutes, every time, which is why it got run at the end of a task rather than during it, exactly when it is least useful. By the end of this session it was **27 checks** with a five-second first tier.
Enumerate from git, not from the filesystem

The gate used to walk the tree with a hand-maintained skip list, and that list had already failed once — an agent worktree carried its own stray copy of the terminology reference and scored six false hits against the actual file that is the authority on those terms. Switching to `git ls-files` needs no denylist at all, because a file has to be tracked to be seen: the false positive becomes structurally impossible rather than merely denied. On this machine, where every filesystem `stat` crosses a virtualisation boundary, it is also dramatically faster — the banned-terms check alone went from **31,906 ms to 1,393 ms**, and the three converted checks together dropped 45.7 seconds off every run.

A GDScript parse check was moved to run before the engine even boots, because a parse error there is a hang or a blank frame, never an error reported at the actual failure site — it had already cost real diagnosis time five separate times in one session before this landed.
Tiers, and the rule that makes them safe

Tier 1 is nine checks in under five seconds and opens no window; tier 2 adds six subsystem checks for about fourteen seconds; tier 3 and tier 4 — all of it, including 1,152-run parity — are what the gate always was. The part that matters more than the speed: a check a tier excludes reports **skip**, with a reason, and stays in the JSON output rather than disappearing from it. An absent entry reads as a pass to anything consuming the file, and a green partial run that looks like a full one is the exact failure this exists to prevent. A `--budget` flag turns each tier's time limit into an assertion, so a tier whose cost silently doubles fails outright instead of quietly stopping being used — which is exactly what caught the next batch of checks below going over budget.
A gate that runs somewhere other than this machine

The whole verification story had lived on one machine with a Windows-side art tool, a Linux engine build and a pile of LFS sprites, so nothing had ever run in continuous integration. The new workflow runs tier 1 — nine checks, about five seconds — on every pull request, checked out with LFS turned off entirely, because tier 1 needs none of those bytes. Its pre-commit and pre-push hooks were written and deliberately left uninstalled: seven agents were committing through this repository at the time, and a hook failing on someone else's in-flight file would have blocked all of them.
Decision 061: the safe operation set was half right

Decision 030 banned square roots from both rule engines, reasoning that Godot's `Vector2` is float32 and its distance function 'is not correctly rounded'. That bundled two different claims, and a probe — 100,000 float64 pairs across five value regimes, run on CPython, Linux Godot and Windows Godot, comparing raw IEEE-754 bytes — found only one of them true. `sqrt` itself matched 100,000 of 100,000 samples on all three runtimes; IEEE-754 requires it to be correctly rounded, and both engines issue the identical instruction for it. The real culprit was `Vector2.distance_to`, a float32 helper: on two million points placed exactly on an integer radius, it disagrees with the equivalent float64 computation on a boundary test **10.2%** of the time. The trigonometric and transcendental functions fared worse still — `tan` diverges between the Windows and Linux/CPython runtimes on **4.32%** of samples, `sin` on 0.133%, `cos` on 0.120%.

The corrected safe set — the four arithmetic operators, `sqrt`, `fmod`, `floor`, `min`/`max` and comparisons — is now a tier-1 gate check that parses both rule files rather than grepping them, because a regex misses an aliased import and false-positives on a comment discussing the banned names. It was proved red three separate ways before being trusted, by breaking each real file in place and restoring it byte-exact: a banned `sin` call, a float32 `distance_to` call, and a rules file quietly referencing an engine-only global that a bare parse check cannot see failing at all. That last one is the subject of its own entry, later in this journal.
Parity got slower before it got faster

Parity is the project's core guarantee and its worst bottleneck, and this session made it worse before making it better: 864 runs at roughly nine minutes when the day opened, 1,152 at roughly ten after four new grading policies and multi-lane paths landed — past the point it could still run inside the tool harness's own command timeout. The fix is a digest over everything that can actually change an outcome: the rule files, every tracked file under `data/`, and the engine binary's own version string, because an engine upgrade can move floating-point behaviour with no repository diff at all. A cache hit is loud about it — the tool prints what it skipped and when it last verified, and the gate reports the check as **skip**, never a silent **ok**. Sharding, when a run is actually needed, uses measured per-anchor cost rather than splitting the anchor list evenly: anchor-24 costs 22.7 seconds against anchor-01's 1.58, a 14.4x spread, and bin-packing against that measurement holds a four-way split to **1.4%** deviation from the mean, against 32.2% for round-robin and 61.5% for a naive contiguous split.

entries.title: Measured, not argued
entries.summary: The numbers a performance change is judged by, taken as seriously as the parity run that proves it changed nothing else: a 2.65x speedup at 64x64, a quadratic draw cost flattened to a constant, a texture limit nobody on this machine had actually measured, and a dimming factor checked to within 8-bit quantisation.

commits.subject: perf(fx): bucket the hit-flash lookup, the one quadratic term in the draw path
perf(view): cull and cache the board, and build drawables once per frame
build(assets): one command, content-hashed, and it stops touching what did not change
fix(fx): brownout dims the fight, which is the whole reason glow is a separate pass

body.text: 'A change that passes verification has only proved it changed nothing observable, which is also what a no-op proves' is a rule this session earned the hard way (see the entry on this day's failures, later in this journal). The discipline it produced shows up everywhere a number gets quoted here: measured, never inferred.
2.65x, at the frame that does not exist yet

The board was drawn with no culling and no caching at all — 4,096 tile draws a frame at 64x64 before a single unit even moved — and the list of everything to draw was rebuilt and re-sorted four times a frame, once per draw layer. Tiles are now cached once per anchor and culled against the camera's visible rectangle; the draw list is built once and shared across all four layers. Measured at 64x64 with 60 emplacements and roughly 530 drawable objects: the board's own draw call goes from **11.13 ms to 4.57 ms**, and the total across all four layers from 14.35 ms to 5.42 ms — a **2.65x** speedup. On today's actual anchors the win is a smaller 1.44x, because the frame was already cheap there; the point of the work is the board that does not exist yet. Five deterministic no-combat frames came back byte-for-byte identical before and after, and so did a full-combat frame.
A quadratic term, bucketed flat

The hit-flash lookup scanned the entire live hit list for every drawn unit — climbing from 9.3 microseconds to 58.1 per call as a standalone benchmark's crowd grew from 150 to 900 units. Bucketing it by tile and searching only the surrounding neighbourhood holds per-call cost flat at **2.2 to 2.9 microseconds** across that same range, proved against 910 differential queries with zero mismatches — including the exact tie-break the original scan preserved by walking ascending indices, which the bucketed version had to reproduce by comparing distance-and-index pairs regardless of which order its buckets happen to be walked in.
A number nobody on this machine had actually measured

`GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE` was assumed rather than known, until an EGL surfaceless probe against the same software rendering stack the game itself uses returned **16384**. The atlas packer's own asserted floor is 4096 — not the GLES 3.0 specification minimum of 2048, because 2048 would already fail the page this project renders today at 3072 px.

body.caption: A combat frame at 152 of 290 MW, no brownout in effect — the baseline a since-fixed bug was measured against. The pooled bolt, arc, beam, flak and mortar effects carried glow and nothing else, so the most emissive thing on screen was the one thing brownout's dimming never touched. Fixed by hoisting one energy term through every draw call in the file; the clean measurement is the field pulse, driven by simulation time rather than by the moment of firing: a background-subtracted ratio of 0.31 against the intended 0.35 factor, inside 8-bit quantisation.

entries.title: Thirty agents, one tree
entries.summary: Roughly thirty agents ran across this session, landing forty-four commits against one shared working tree — the same directory the owner plays the game out of while agents edit it. Most of what makes that survivable turned out to be process, not code.

commits.subject: docs: a slow command is not failed, it is backgrounded — and that bills
feat(tooling): the reaper knows what it is killing, and captures are bounded
docs(skill): the wrap reaps last, not first, when agents are still out
feat(hooks): turn six remembered rules into mechanical ones

body.text: Roughly thirty agents ran across this session, landing forty-four commits against one shared working tree — the same directory the owner plays the game out of while agents edit it. Most of what makes that survivable is process, not code, and it is worth recording as its own kind of result.
A slow command is not failed, it is billed

Four separate agents in one session stopped mid-task, apparently stuck, waiting on a command none of them had chosen to background: a long screenshot capture, a nine-minute parity run, and two others. None of them were actually hung. The tool harness's default two-minute timeout does not fail a slow command, it silently detaches it — and a detached process the harness is still tracking re-invokes the agent when it finally exits, billing a session everyone involved believed was already over. The fix is procedural rather than a code change: know in advance which commands can run long, and give those an explicit timeout up front rather than accepting the default.
Captures multiply, they do not parallelise

A single screenshot capture on this machine's software renderer measured at 788% CPU — about eight of sixteen cores. Three running at once drove load average to 18.6 and turned a nine-second capture into minutes, which is how two agents independently ran into the same two-minute command timeout on what looked like ordinary work. Captures are now bounded to two concurrent, machine-wide, through a lease file rather than a remembered rule.
The reaper learned what it is allowed to kill

Cleaning up stray processes at the end of a session used to classify anything that looked like a leftover engine process as fair game to kill — and across one seven-agent stretch, a report-only run of that cleanup repeatedly listed six to eight processes belonging to **other agents**, mid-capture, that an unconditional kill would have ended outright. Every process launch now takes a lease file naming its owner, and a cleanup pass walks a stray process's parent chain back to the lease that owns it before deciding whether it is abandoned or simply busy.

The honest limit found while building it: the session identifier this environment exposes is shared by every agent a single session fans out into, not unique per agent, so a kill command still cannot fully tell 'abandoned' from 'a sibling's live work'. That is why only the coordinating agent ever runs the kill command, and only after every fanned-out agent has already reported back.
Six rules, turned mechanical

Every rule above had already been written down once, in the project's own working instructions, before this session started — and every one of them still failed at least once anyway, because a rule someone has to remember under pressure is a rule that eventually gets skipped. All six became hooks that run automatically rather than guidance that has to be recalled: writes to the engine's import cache are denied outright, a long-running command with no explicit timeout gets a warning, and git's stash, add, reset and checkout-with-a-path are all denied with no escape hatch, because a plain path-scoped commit already covers the one legitimate need those commands are ever reached for. Whether the hooks actually fire on a live edit was left an open question rather than assumed answered — a prior attempt at a similar hook was never once observed firing, apparently because the tool harness reads its own configuration only at the start of a session.

entries.title: The failures, given real weight
entries.summary: A journal that only records what worked is a lie by omission. Four things went wrong this session, each recorded here in the same detail as anything that shipped clean: a fix that did nothing, a stash that hit five workstreams, a one-line change that broke parity in the least visible way possible, and an atlas that quietly rendered every sprite as flat grey.

commits.subject: docs: the working tree is shared, so git stash is friendly fire
perf(rules): stop _covered_by() walking every emplacement per unit per tick
fix(rules): an autoload in anchor_sim.gd returns 1152 empty parity rows
fix(art): the Hollow's lit cones sit on the dark cones' axis, and the manifest gets hashes

body.text: A journal that only records what worked is a lie by omission. Four things went wrong this session, and each is recorded here in the same detail as anything that shipped clean.
Decision 058: a fix that passed 864-run parity and did nothing

An idle emplacement re-scanning every unit forever — the first defect named in the measurement entry earlier in this journal — had a proposed fix: retry on the next tick rather than the same one. It was implemented in both rule engines. It passed parity across **864 runs**. It changed nothing at all — measured, not argued: stripping the change back out left a full detailed grade of all 24 anchors and three difficulties byte-identical, **27,138 lines**. The reason is arithmetic rather than a mistake in the code: the value the fix scheduled for the next tick was already the value the current tick would hold one step later, so the retry it added was already happening on its own. The one change that would have actually skipped real work — a longer retry interval — would have been a balance change wearing a performance change's clothing, and nobody had signed up to make that call casually. The fix was removed rather than kept as a harmless comment, because dead code sitting in the hottest loop of the rules, mirrored across two languages forever, is not free, and a reader would reasonably assume it does something.

The wider point is why this is a journal entry rather than a line in a commit message: a change that passes verification has only proved it changed nothing observable — which is exactly what a no-op also proves. A separate benchmarking tool exists now specifically so the other half of any performance claim, the actual gain, has to be measured too, not just its safety.
A stash that swept eleven files across five workstreams

An agent working alongside several others ran `git stash` to get a clean baseline for a before/after comparison. It took eleven files belonging to five different pieces of work with it and left the shared tree looking exactly like the last commit. For several minutes, every other agent in that tree was reading committed history instead of its own uncommitted edits — which raises no error at all, it just quietly makes any measurement taken in that window describe code nobody had actually written. It was recovered because the stash happened to get popped again, not because anything caught it in the moment.

The rule that came out of it: an agent never runs `stash`, `reset`, `checkout` with a path, or `add`. A coordinator commits with a path-scoped commit inside a lock-retry loop instead, and a proper worktree-per-workstream setup is the actual fix that makes the whole class of mistake structurally impossible rather than merely against the rules.
A one-line change that returned 1,152 empty parity rows

Wiring the last of nine recovery effects looked like a one-line read inside the rules file. It took the parity harness down instead: the harness preloads the rules with no autoloads available at all, so one reference to an autoloaded singleton made the whole rules file fail to **load** — not fail a test, fail to load — and every one of 1,152 parity runs came back as an empty result, which then crashed the harness itself on a lookup that named the harness, not the actual bug. Meanwhile the ordinary parse check stayed green throughout the entire episode, because it resolves autoloads from the project configuration and the runtime parity harness does not. The fix follows a standing rule directly: a recovery effect has to transform the simulation's inputs, never reach into a live singleton, and it was rewritten that way in one line once the actual cause was finally found.
The atlas that made everything flat grey

Raising the sprite cell size to 512 px was tested end to end — the render pipeline converges at that size, the packed page fits comfortably under this machine's measured texture-size ceiling, and a full library rebuild takes about two and a half minutes. Every real material in the game rendered as flat placeholder grey anyway, because a separate constant elsewhere in the engine still hardcoded the old 128x64 tile size, and the sprite loader's own size check failed silently into its placeholder path instead of raising an error. This was caught by sampling actual pixel colour against the expected material colour, not by looking at the frame — which is the only way it would have been caught at all, because a uniformly grey board reads, at a glance, exactly like a lighting change rather than a broken asset pipeline. The change was reverted back to 256 px and a real render was verified again before anything was reported as working.

entries.title: An anchor has lanes, not a lane
entries.summary: Anchor JSON carried one path array, and both rule engines were built around a single point lookup, one path length, and a leak test of distance against it. Two to five simultaneous lanes — the thing that makes a front line exist at all — needed that structure to move first, and the most important bug this session found was invisible until it did.

commits.subject: fix(art): one yaw count, and a hysteresis band that survives changing it
feat(rules): an anchor has lanes, not a lane
balance(anchor-09): make the flank lane a decision, not a tax
fix(rules): furthest along means furthest along its own lane

body.text: Anchor JSON carried one `path` array, and both rule engines were built around a single point-lookup function, one path length, and a leak test of distance travelled against it. Two to five simultaneous lanes and up to four spawn points — the thing that makes a front line exist at all — needed that structure to move first, and it was the blocker behind fifteen other war-economy issues.
Decision 059: lanes are an index, never a name

`path` became `paths` — an array of id-and-waypoints objects — and every rule that touches a lane takes a required integer index into that array, never the string id. A default index would have let a missed call site compile and quietly assume lane zero, which is the one failure mode that could have survived every check in this repository: the game would run, parity would pass, and units on a second lane would silently walk the first lane's geometry. Ten internal call sites were updated to require the index explicitly, with no fallback.

The migration itself is proved, not asserted. A tool converts every existing single-lane anchor into a one-entry `paths` array with no lane key added anywhere, and a full detailed grade of all 24 anchors taken before the migration diffs **empty** against one taken after — 35,356 lines, zero differences. 'A single-lane anchor is the degenerate case of a multi-lane one' is now something measured rather than assumed true.
Decision 060: one yaw count, and a hysteresis fraction

The number of sprite facing directions was written independently in three separate places, and the constant that keeps a facing from flickering between two buckets — 12.0 degrees — was already larger than half a bucket at sixteen directions (11.25 degrees), which would have frozen every emplacement's facing permanently the moment that count was ever raised, with no visible sign of what had gone wrong. The constant became a fraction of a bucket instead of a fixed number of degrees, correct at any yaw count by construction rather than by coincidence. Measured on a real combat replay: at four directions, the new hysteresis cut facing reversals from 21 to 16 out of 84 total changes; at sixteen directions, from 90 reversals in 307 changes down to 59 in 263. No setting reached zero changes — which is the number that would have meant a frozen facing, the exact failure this exists to prevent.
Decision 062: furthest along means furthest along its own lane

The most consequential finding multi-lane paths exposed, and it was invisible until they existed. Targeting picked the furthest-advanced reachable unit by raw distance travelled along its own lane, compared directly across lanes with no normalisation at all. anchor-09's main lane is 37 tiles and its flank is 14 — so any gun that could see both lanes targeted the main lane almost exclusively from the moment a main-lane unit passed 14 tiles in, about eight seconds into every wave. The flank slots were never actually defending the flank; they only looked like they could on a chart of raw distance.

The fix compares progress as a fraction of each unit's own lane length rather than raw distance. The intuitive-sounding alternative — remaining distance to the exit — was checked and rejected on measurement, not on taste: it **inverts** the bug rather than fixing it, because the flank's remaining distance is capped at 14, so a live flank unit would outrank a main-lane unit anywhere across 62% of that lane, regardless of how far the main-lane unit had actually travelled. Single-lane boards are untouched by construction, since a fraction of a constant preserves order — proved across all 23 single-lane anchors, byte-identical across the full 24-anchor detailed grade.

body.caption: anchor-09 mid-wave, the tactical map in the corner making both lanes readable at once — the main path down the centre and the flank pulled off to one side. The dialogue line ('That's not our load. They're taking it off u') is the moment the flank lane's own threat becomes legible rather than theoretical.

body.text: Landing the fix left anchor-09 unwinnable at hard and brutal — from 9 of 16 winning builds down to zero, and 6 of 16 down to zero — because its acceptance case had deliberately been left light, to prove the plumbing rather than to be a finished level. It grades clean now at all three difficulties, and the fix was not the coverage split it first looked like: two slots were placed where a tower physically cannot see the main lane at all, which is what makes their targeting exclusively the flank's, and the flank's own wave timing was widened to match. Only anchor-09 moved in the full 1,152-run parity comparison, and no cell flipped a result — one policy still wins, at 3 lives instead of 4, with one more leak, which reads as attention genuinely split between two lanes rather than one lane being ignored entirely.

entries.title: Terrain, and a denominator that had to survive free placement
entries.summary: Two pieces of foundation that nothing is built on top of yet, deliberately, so each stays provably correct in isolation: elevation as regions and ramps rather than a dense grid, and a board-saturation guard rewritten before the thing it used to divide by is deleted out from under it.

commits.subject: feat(data): terrain shape, and a fixture that stops the two parsers drifting
feat(validate): terrain invariants a schema cannot express, and the upgrade draw
feat(validate): a saturation denominator that survives free placement

body.text: Decision 057: terrain as regions and ramps, never a dense grid by default

An anchor needed to carry elevation without breaking either of the two independent parsers that read anchor JSON — one in the reference engine, one in the game engine — silently disagreeing on some tile nine minutes into a parity run, surfacing as an unexplained leak with no pointer to terrain anywhere in it. The shape settled on is regions and ramps: rectangles that paint in array order, a later rectangle completely overwriting whatever an earlier one covered, including lowering it — with a dense heightmap available as an escape hatch for a future board generator, replacing regions entirely rather than blending with them.

A shared fixture resolves the same terrain description through both parsers and diffs the result tile-for-tile against a hand-authored expected grid, and against each other, deliberately on a non-square board so a row/column swap in either parser cannot hide behind symmetry. It was proved to fail loudly, too: deliberately corrupting one tile makes both resolvers report the mismatch rather than agreeing quietly on the wrong answer. One anchor carries a pilot terrain description now; it grades identically to before, which is true by construction — nothing in the rules reads terrain yet.

A follow-on pass added the checks a schema cannot express on its own: every elevation value has to sit inside the declared number of levels, a ramp's two ends have to actually differ by exactly one level and match the resolved grid on both sides, and no build slot may sit on a ramp or a cliff face. All eleven of its fixtures were proved to fail for the right reason before being trusted. The same pass also fixed the board-saturation guard reading only a tower's base power draw and never its upgraded draw — invisible until a tower's upgrade costs meaningfully more than its base form does, exactly the shape this programme's later spectacle weapons are specified to have.
Decision 063: a denominator that survives removing the thing it divided by

The board-saturation guard — the check that stops a level from quietly deleting its own power decision by letting every slot run flat out — divided by the number of build slots. Free placement removes slots entirely, and a divide with nothing to divide by would have stopped guarding **silently**, on exactly the failure it exists to catch: one anchor had already once reached 103% of what running every slot at maximum draw would cost, while still grading as perfectly winnable, because a level with no power decision left in it is still a level you can win.

The fix is an authored integer cap, required by the schema whenever slots are absent and optional — falling back to the slot count — whenever slots are still present. That is why this changed **none** of the 24 existing anchors' numbers; every one of them takes the fallback branch and reproduces its existing figure exactly. It was proved to fail four different ways through the schema's own fixture mechanism before being trusted: an anchor with neither a slot list nor a cap is rejected outright, the same anchor with a cap and zero slots passes cleanly (which is the entire point), and inflating a cap back up to the old failing ratio reproduces the original failure exactly.

The corresponding change inside the two rule engines is written out call site by call site but was not applied in this same change, because those files were being rewritten by another workstream at the time. One trap was identified and has to land in the same future change: a build call inside the parity test harness does not check its own return value, which is safe only as long as a build request can never be refused. The moment a cap can refuse one, that becomes an infinite loop instead of a bug.

entries.title: What the player can do now that they could not this morning
entries.summary: Three changes, each closing a gap between what the game could already do internally and what a person sitting at the keyboard could actually reach: a tactical map for a board too big to see all at once, a way to give the board back at maximum interface scale, and a campaign system that had existed for two sessions without ever once being reachable by playing.

commits.subject: feat(ui): give the board back — a hide-panels toggle, and one warning silenced
feat(ui): a tactical map, because the board stopped fitting on the screen
feat(game): winning an anchor takes you to the draft, and the draft talks back

body.text: Three changes this session, each closing a gap between what the game could already do internally and what a person sitting at the keyboard could actually reach.
A tactical map, because the board stopped fitting on the screen

With lanes now able to number up to five and boards heading past 48x48, a single screen reading lane pressure stopped being enough. The minimap draws the board's own silhouette, every lane's route, a threat wash bucketed by how much a leaking unit actually costs rather than by raw unit count — because one heavy unit is not worth the same life as one light one — plus emplacement marks, unit dots, and the camera's own viewing rectangle. Online and offline emplacements are shape-coded rather than colour-coded, filled against hollow, verified by converting a real capture to greyscale and confirming the distinction still reads clearly with colour removed entirely.

body.caption: The minimap live on a board in progress. Emplacements online read as filled rings, not by colour alone, which is what makes the distinction survive a greyscale conversion — an accessibility check taken seriously rather than assumed to already be fine.

A kill chain building past five hits (the CHAIN x5 readout, top left) while the bus runs 11% over its capacity — the map holding the wide read of where the pressure is while the panel and the fight itself hold the close one.

body.text: Hiding the panels costs information, never the ability to act

At 200% interface scale the two instrument panels do not crowd anchor-24's board, they erase all but four pixels of it. A hide toggle was built rather than a responsive layout, because narrowing the panels cannot fix a four-pixel strip, and because a toggle is the kind of thing a player deliberately reaches for, where a width-based layout would need no input action at all. Every verb a player has — build, sell, upgrade, targeting, tower cycling, all three abilities — was traced and confirmed to route from board input straight into the simulation, never through a HUD widget, so hiding the panels was confirmed to cost only readouts: bus load, funds, lives, the datasheet, ability charge, incoming composition. One hint chip stays on screen while everything else is hidden, because the way back must never be the thing that disappears with it.
Winning an anchor finally takes you to the draft

The recovery draft between anchors — pick one of three permanent campaign bonuses, the other two lost to the level just cleared — has existed in the data and the schema for two sessions and had never once been reachable by actually playing the game. The win handler skipped straight to reloading the next anchor. It now goes to the draft screen instead, without touching which anchor was selected, so the draft grades the anchor just won and its button reads DEBRIEF rather than NEXT.

body.caption: The draft screen, reached by actually winning anchor-01 rather than by navigating to it directly — ten of ten lives held, three recovery cards on offer, only one of which survives past this choice.

The screen after a card is taken. The reaction dialogue — previously written but with no anchor's dialog file able to properly host a line meant to play after every level, rather than one level's coincidence — now has a home of its own, read directly by the draft screen instead of borrowed from anchor-01's file.

body.text: Proving the fix end to end surfaced one real engine trap along the way: a global flag this project uses to pause frame capture during a screenshot is engine-wide state, not scoped to one scene, so a scene transition happening mid-capture left the next scene's own capture waiting forever for a frame that had already been told not to render. That is now a known trap rather than a mystery the next capture-during-transition would have hit cold.

entries.title: Closing the loop
entries.summary: The last change of the session was about work being visible somewhere other than a commit log: a close verb for finished issues, and this journal itself.

commits.subject: feat: close the loop on GitHub, and start recording the journey

body.text: The last change of the session was about work being visible somewhere other than a commit log.

The issue-projection tool had a create verb and a sync verb, and no verb for finished, so the projection onto GitHub could only ever grow. Twenty-nine of this session's issue specs were implemented, verified and committed while every one of their corresponding issues sat open on GitHub, and the owner noticed before the tooling did. A close verb now exists, and it requires a note: what landed, and how it was proved — because a bare close leaves the evidence sitting in a commit message nobody browsing the issue would ever think to go find. Twenty-nine specs closed this way; forty-five stayed open.

And this journal. It exists because a commit log is a fine record of what changed and a poor one of why any of it mattered, or of what went wrong along the way. Two rules apply to it going forward, the same two that already apply to the project's own decision record: it is append-only, so a later entry that overturns something written here says so and links back rather than quietly editing history, and the failures stay in — a journal that only records what worked is a lie by omission, and this session gave the entry on that subject, earlier in this journal, plenty of material to prove it with. It publishes as committed, pre-generated HTML with no build step at all, deliberately, so there is no toolchain here that can rot between now and whoever reads it next.
